title: Python GIS at UoA
text:
GISCI 343 at UoA
Welcome to the course!
This is an online workbook for the GISCI 343 course called Geospatial Data Science, launched in 2026.
This is course designed and delivered by Dr. Hyesop Shin from the School of Environment at the University of Auckland, New Zealand.
Unlike conventional GIS coursework that focuses on tools or isolated techniques, this book goes beyond the standard GIS and Python combination. The emphasis is on building applied, production-oriented skills that reflect how geospatial data science is practised outside the classroom, particularly through dashboards and Python packaging.
The book is organised into three main parts:
Part 1. Doing geospatial analysis using Python (Weeks 1-5)
Part 2. Creating geospatial dashboards (Weeks 6-8)
Part 3. Publishing Python packages with a geospatial focus (Weeks 9-12)
Throughout the course, Positron is used as the primary development environment.

title: Python GIS at UoA
text:
Who is this for?
This book is designed for students and learners who already have foundational GIS knowledge, such as introductory GIS or remote sensing courses, but who have limited exposure to programming.
If you are familiar with any dataframe-based workflow, most examples should be approachable. Familiarity with Pandas will be particularly helpful, as all Polars examples are accompanied by equivalent Pandas implementations for comparison and learning.
Reading Modern Pandas is not required, although it is a recommended resource for those who wish to deepen their understanding.

title: Python GIS at UoA
text:
Why this approach?
Although artificial intelligence has transformed how we learn, analyse data, and write code, reproducibility and sound practice in data science remain essential.
Simply combining GIS and Python is no longer sufficient. This course therefore addresses broader and often overlooked questions:

Why do we use Git, and how does it support reproducible research?






Note



Git provides a transparent and traceable record of how a project evolves over time. Every change to code, data processing logic, or documentation is recorded, allowing results to be reproduced, audited, and revisited. This is essential for geospatial data science, where analytical outcomes often depend on many interlinked steps, such as data cleaning, spatial joins, projections, and modelling assumptions.
Using Git encourages good research habits: small, well-documented changes, clear reasoning behind decisions, and the ability to roll back or compare different analytical approaches. In collaborative settings, Git also enables multiple contributors to work on the same project without overwriting each other’s work, making it the backbone of reproducible and open geospatial research.




Why do we build dashboards, and how do they help communicate results to practitioners and decision makers?






Note



Dashboards transform analytical outputs into interactive and interpretable artefacts. Rather than presenting static maps or tables, dashboards allow users to explore spatial patterns, filter scenarios, and ask their own questions. This is particularly important in applied geospatial work, where stakeholders may not be familiar with code but need to engage with evidence.
By building dashboards, students learn how to bridge the gap between analysis and communication. Dashboards force careful thinking about what results matter, how uncertainty is presented, and how spatial information can be explored intuitively. These skills are essential when working with planners, policymakers, and industry partners who rely on clear, actionable insights rather than raw analytical outputs.




Why do we develop Python packages as a final project, and how does this introduce object-oriented programming with a clear purpose and real-world relevance?






Note



Developing a Python package shifts the focus from writing one-off scripts to building reusable, maintainable software. Packaging requires students to structure code logically, define clear interfaces, and think about how others will use their work. This naturally introduces object-oriented programming concepts, such as abstraction, encapsulation, and modular design, in a context where they serve a practical purpose.
In geospatial data science, packaging allows analytical workflows, spatial utilities, or modelling components to be shared, tested, and extended. The final package becomes a tangible output that can be included in a portfolio, reused in future projects, or published openly. This mirrors professional practice and helps students understand how geospatial tools are developed, maintained, and deployed in real-world environments.


Each of these components is intentionally included to help students understand professional workflows and to produce outputs that can be shared beyond the university setting.
The three modules in this book are designed to be complete, reusable, and ready to engage with society, forming a practical portfolio that reflects contemporary geospatial data science practice.

Exercise 1: Create a GIS project

import geopandas as gpd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from shapely.geometry import Point

# Create GeoDataFrame
cities = gpd.GeoDataFrame({
    'city': ['Auckland', 'Wellington', 'Christchurch'],

title: 2.2. DataFrames and Pandas
text:
Introduction
In Section 2.1, you learned Python fundamentals: lists for storing sequences, loops for iteration, and conditionals for decision-making. Now we’ll build on those foundations to work with structured tabular data—the kind you’d see in Excel spreadsheets or GIS attribute tables.
This section introduces: - Dictionaries: Flexible key-value structures (essential for GeoJSON and APIs) - pandas DataFrames: Python’s answer to spreadsheets and database tables - Data operations: Reading, filtering, grouping, and transforming data
Why this matters for GIS: Most spatial analysis involves attribute data alongside geometry. You’ll spend significant time manipulating tables before (or after) spatial operations. These skills are foundational for Section 2.4 (GeoPandas), where you’ll add spatial capabilities to DataFrames.
The progression: - Section 2.1: Basics (lists, loops, if/else) - Section 2.2: Structured data (dictionaries, DataFrames, operations) - Section 2.3: Visualisation (making sense of your data) - Section 2.4: Spatial data (adding geography)

title: Interactive Dashboards with Shiny for Python
text:
Overview
Web-based dashboards have revolutionised how we communicate geospatial analysis. Instead of static maps and reports, dashboards allow users to explore data dynamically—filtering, zooming, and interacting with visualisations in real time. This chapter introduces Shiny for Python, a powerful framework for building interactive web applications without requiring extensive web development experience.
You’ll learn to create professional dashboards that combine interactive maps, responsive controls, and analytical outputs—perfect for communicating urban analytics insights to policymakers, stakeholders, and the public.

title: Interactive Dashboards with Shiny for Python
text:
What You Will Learn
This chapter covers:

WebGIS Fundamentals (?sec-webgis-wasm-shiny): Understanding web mapping, file formats, and WebAssembly (WASM) for browser-based applications
Shiny Architecture (5  Shiny Functions and Reactivity): The UI/server model, reactive programming, and building responsive interfaces
Routing and Congestion (6  Routing and Congestion Analysis): Analysing transport networks, travel times, and congestion indicators
Origin-Destination Analysis (7  Origin-Destination Analysis): Understanding and visualising movement patterns between locations
Network Analysis (8  Network Analysis for GIS): Working with street networks using OSMnx and city2graph for accessibility analysis
Dashboard Development (?sec-shiny-assignment): Building and deploying complete multi-page applications

To install packages

Traditional Python took a system-wide approach with global installations and limited isolation, leading to “works on my machine” problems, dependency conflicts, and difficult onboarding.


new in 2026 uv installation
Traditionally, we used pip, pip-tools, pipx, poetry, pyenv, or virtualenv to install packages. And so have we taught pip (!pip in colab) for our GISCI 343 course. In the recent years, however, developers have used multi-thread languages such as Rust to speed up the installation process.
Users have reported significant time savings when using uv pip install instead of pip install for such environments. For example, one benchmark installing the pandas package showed:

title: 3.1 Web GIS, WASM, and Shiny
section: Static Maps: Why We Still Use Them
text:
Static Maps: Why We Still Use Them
The good part about static maps is the author controls exactly what the viewer sees. Static mapping supports precise control over symbolisation, classification, layout, annotation, and visual hierarchy, which is central to cartographic design and thematic mapping. Moreover, because static maps serve as a fixed record. They are excellent for legal documents, historical archives, or reports where you need to show exactly what the data looked like on a specific date without it updating automatically.
Take central Auckland as an example. You can see that the ‘Reds’ have a high population density and the ‘Greens’ have a low population density per mesh block (a small geographic unit used in the census), which fades away the further you go from the city.

Another advantage is that it provides one narrative message. No zooming or panning around, just print out and the map-maker can guide the viewer’s eye to the specific story or “message” of the map without distractions.
No internet required. Often times, we don’t realise that webmaps (OpenStreetMaps) run under the internet. But static maps, you only need a code chunk and a computer - that is it!

title: 3.1 Web GIS, WASM, and Shiny
section: Static Maps - Where They Fall Short
text:
Static Maps - Where They Fall Short
Zero Interactivity: Users can’t click a feature to see more metadata, toggle layers on and off, or change the base map to get more context.
“Frozen” Data: The moment a static map is exported, the data begins to age. If the underlying data changes (e.g., real-time traffic or weather), the map becomes obsolete almost instantly.
Scale Restrictions: You are stuck with the scale the creator chose. If you want to see the street-level detail on a national-level static map, you’re out of luck—it just becomes a blur of pixels.
Information Overload: Since you can’t “filter” a static map, trying to show too many variables at once often leads to a cluttered, unreadable mess.

title: 3.1 Web GIS, WASM, and Shiny
section: Seriously, which files should I use
text:
Seriously, which files should I use
It is a classic WebGIS dilemma: GeoJSON is technically “worse” (larger, slower, memory-heavy) but “better” for the web.

In the area of Geographic Information Systems (GIS), the choice of data format significantly impacts data management, interoperability, and overall project efficiency.

According to the Medium blog by Felipe Limeira (medium blog, Oct 2024), while GeoPackage (GPKG) is the superior choice for comprehensive data management and performance, GeoJSON remains the “de facto” standard for web applications and real-time data exchange.
Here is why GeoJSON is still the king of the web despite being “clunky”:

It Speaks “Native” JavaScript The “JSON” in GeoJSON stands for JavaScript Object Notation. Because almost all WebGIS applications (Leaflet, Mapbox, OpenLayers) are built with JavaScript, GeoJSON is natively understood.

No “Translator” needed: To use a GeoPackage in a browser, you often need a complex library (like sql.js) to “read” the SQLite database. With GeoJSON, the browser just sees it as a standard JavaScript object. It’s ready to use the moment it’s downloaded.

Human-Readability & Debugging If a web map isn’t loading correctly, you can open a GeoJSON file in any text editor (or the browser console) and read it like a sentence.

Instant Verification: You can see exactly which attribute is broken or where a coordinate is misplaced. You can’t do that with the binary “blob” of a GeoPackage or the multiple cryptic files of a Shapefile.

Web API Dominance Most modern web services (APIs) communicate via JSON. If you are building a WebGIS that pulls live weather data, transit locations, or social media check-ins, that data is almost certainly arriving as GeoJSON. It fits perfectly into the “REST API” architecture of the modern internet.
Version Control Friendly (GitHub) Because GeoJSON is text-based, it works beautifully with version control systems like Git.

Track Changes: You can see exactly which line (feature) changed in a “diff.” Binary formats like GPKG or SHP are “black boxes” to Git; if you change one coordinate, the whole file looks different to the system.

Simplicity for Small Datasets For a map showing 50 coffee shop locations, the overhead of setting up a SQLite-based GeoPackage is overkill. A GeoJSON is a single, “dumb” file that “just works.”










Format
Description
Key Strengths
Key Limitations




Shapefile (.shp)
Historically the dominant vector format in GIS, now largely obsolete but still widely used in legacy systems and data portals.
Broad software support; simple and familiar format.
2 GB file size limit; fragmented across multiple files (.shp, .dbf, .shx, .prj); limited attribute typing and encoding support; no native support for topology or multiple layers.


GeoPackage (.gpkg)
An OGC standard built on SQLite, optimised for efficient storage, indexing, and local spatial analysis.
Compact single-file container; fast read and write performance; supports multiple layers and spatial indexing; strong support in desktop GIS and Python workflows.
Not natively readable by web browsers; requires server-side processing or conversion for WebGIS delivery.


GeoJSON (.geojson)
A JSON-based vector format designed for interoperability and web-based data exchange.
Native compatibility with JavaScript and web mapping libraries; human-readable and easy to debug; ideal for APIs and lightweight data delivery.
Larger file size; slower parsing and higher memory use; inefficient for large datasets and complex geometries.

title: 2.4 Urban analytics indicators
text:
Introduction
Urban indicators are the building blocks of understanding how cities work. Think of them as the vital signs of urban life – just as a doctor measures heart rate and blood pressure, urban analysts measure density, accessibility, and connectivity to diagnose how well a city is functioning. In this chapter, we’ll focus on computing meaningful indicators for Auckland and learning how to interpret them responsibly.
Why does this matter? Well-chosen indicators can reveal patterns invisible to the naked eye: which neighbourhoods lack green space access, where pedestrian activity concentrates, or how street networks facilitate movement. These insights directly inform urban planning decisions – from where to build new parks to how to design low-emission zones (shin2022assessing?).

title: 2.4 Urban analytics indicators
text:
Population density: The foundation
Population density is perhaps the most fundamental urban indicator. It’s simply the number of people per unit area, typically expressed as persons per km². But simple doesn’t mean simplistic – density reveals patterns of urbanisation, housing pressure, and service demand.

Computing density
Let’s calculate population density for Auckland meshblocks:

import geopandas as gpd
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt


# Load Auckland census data
meshblocks = gpd.read_file("data/auckland_meshblocks.gpkg")

# Calculate area in km²
meshblocks['area_km2'] = meshblocks.geometry.area / 1_000_000

# Calculate population density
meshblocks['pop_density'] = meshblocks['population'] / meshblocks['area_km2']

# View the results
print(meshblocks[['meshblock_id', 'population', 'area_km2', 'pop_density']].head())







Important caveats




Units matter! Always check whether your coordinates are in metres, degrees, or something else. For Auckland, NZGD2000 / New Zealand Transverse Mercator 2000 (EPSG:2193) uses metres.
Zero-area problem: Some meshblocks might have very small areas, leading to unrealistic density values. Filter these out or handle them carefully.
Residential vs. total area: Density can be misleading in industrial or commercial zones with few residents but large areas.





Visualising density



fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 1, figsize=(12, 10))

meshblocks.plot(column='pop_density', 
                ax=ax,
                legend=True,
                scheme='quantiles',  # Use quantiles for better distribution
                k=5,  # 5 classes
                cmap='YlOrRd',
                edgecolor='grey',
                linewidth=0.1)

ax.set_title('Population Density in Auckland (persons/km²)', fontsize=14)
ax.set_axis_off()

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()


Figure 1









Interpretation tip



High density doesn’t automatically mean “bad” or “good”. Auckland’s CBD shows extremely high density, which supports walkability and public transport viability. Conversely, some suburban areas have very low density, which can make service provision expensive but offers larger living spaces. Context is everything.

title: 2.4 Urban analytics indicators
section: Access to green space: Distance proxies
text:
Access to green space: Distance proxies
Access to parks and green spaces is crucial for physical activity, mental health, and urban liveability (who2016urban?). We can approximate access by calculating the distance from each residential area to the nearest park.

Finding nearest park distance

from scipy.spatial import cKDTree

# Load parks data
parks = gpd.read_file("data/auckland_parks.gpkg")

# Ensure both datasets use the same CRS
meshblocks = meshblocks.to_crs(epsg=2193)
parks = parks.to_crs(epsg=2193)

# Get centroids of meshblocks
meshblock_points = np.array(list(meshblocks.geometry.centroid.apply(lambda x: (x.x, x.y))))
park_points = np.array(list(parks.geometry.centroid.apply(lambda x: (x.x, x.y))))

# Build KD-tree for efficient nearest neighbour search
tree = cKDTree(park_points)

# Find nearest park for each meshblock
distances, indices = tree.query(meshblock_points, k=1)

# Add distance to dataframe (in metres)
meshblocks['nearest_park_m'] = distances

# Convert to kilometres for readability
meshblocks['nearest_park_km'] = meshblocks['nearest_park_m'] / 1000

print(f"Mean distance to nearest park: {meshblocks['nearest_park_km'].mean():.2f} km")
print(f"Median distance to nearest park: {meshblocks['nearest_park_km'].median():.2f} km")



Caveats and limitations
This “straight-line” distance (Euclidean distance) is a proxy for true accessibility. Real-world access involves:

Network distance: How far you actually walk along streets (usually 20-40% longer than straight-line distance)
Barriers: Motorways, rivers, and railways can make nearby parks difficult to reach
Park quality: A tiny pocket park and a large regional park both count as “nearest park”
Perceptions: Perceived safety and amenities affect whether people actually use parks







Note



For your assignment on pedestrian footfall, consider: Do areas with better park access show different pedestrian patterns? Could parks act as destinations or origins for walking trips?

title: 2.4 Urban analytics indicators
text:
Aggregating to larger zones
Often we want to summarise indicators at larger geographical units – suburbs, wards, or custom analysis zones. Here’s how to aggregate meshblock data to suburbs:

# Load suburbs boundaries
suburbs = gpd.read_file("data/auckland_suburbs.gpkg")

# Spatial join: which meshblocks fall in which suburbs?
meshblocks_with_suburb = gpd.sjoin(meshblocks, suburbs, how='left', predicate='within')

# Aggregate to suburb level
suburb_summary = meshblocks_with_suburb.groupby('suburb_name').agg({
    'population': 'sum',
    'area_km2': 'sum',
    'nearest_park_km': 'mean',  # Mean distance across meshblocks
}).reset_index()

# Recalculate density at suburb level
suburb_summary['pop_density'] = suburb_summary['population'] / suburb_summary['area_km2']

print(suburb_summary.sort_values('pop_density', ascending=False).head())

This aggregation lets you compare suburbs:

# Compare CBD suburbs vs suburban areas
cbd_suburbs = suburb_summary[suburb_summary['suburb_name'].isin(['Auckland Central', 'Grafton', 'Newmarket'])]
suburban = suburb_summary[suburb_summary['suburb_name'].isin(['Albany', 'Howick', 'Papakura'])]

print("\nCBD areas:")
print(cbd_suburbs[['suburb_name', 'pop_density', 'nearest_park_km']])

print("\nSuburban areas:")
print(suburban[['suburb_name', 'pop_density', 'nearest_park_km']])

title: 2.4 Urban analytics indicators
text:
Urban morphology using momepy
Urban morphology studies the form and structure of cities. The momepy package (fleischmann2019momepy?) provides tools to quantify urban form characteristics like street connectivity, building patterns, and block structure. This is particularly relevant for understanding pedestrian movement – more connected street networks generally support more walkability.

Installing and importing momepy

# Install if needed: pip install momepy
import momepy
import networkx as nx



Street network analysis
Let’s analyse Auckland’s street network to identify which streets are most important for pedestrian movement:

# Load street network (you might use OSMnx to download this)
import osmnx as ox

# Download Auckland CBD street network
place_name = "Auckland CBD, New Zealand"
G = ox.graph_from_place(place_name, network_type='walk')

# Convert to GeoDataFrame
edges = ox.graph_to_gdfs(G, nodes=False)
nodes = ox.graph_to_gdfs(G, nodes=True)

# Calculate basic network metrics
edges['length'] = edges.geometry.length

# Calculate betweenness centrality - which streets are on the most paths?
# This can take a while for large networks
betweenness = nx.betweenness_centrality(G, weight='length', normalized=True)

# Add centrality to edges
nodes['betweenness'] = nodes.index.map(betweenness)




# Visualise
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 1, figsize=(12, 12))

edges.plot(ax=ax, color='lightgrey', linewidth=0.5)
nodes.plot(column='betweenness', 
           ax=ax, 
           cmap='Reds', 
           markersize=20,
           legend=True)

ax.set_title('Street Betweenness Centrality in Auckland CBD', fontsize=14)
ax.set_axis_off()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()


Figure 2









What does betweenness centrality tell us?



Streets with high betweenness centrality are “important” in the network – many shortest paths pass through them. In pedestrian studies, these are the streets where you’d expect to see the most footfall, all else being equal. Sound familiar? This connects directly to your assignment!




Calculating reach and closeness

# Reach: How many other nodes can you reach within a given distance?
# This simulates walkable catchment areas

def calculate_reach(G, distance=800):  # 800m = ~10 minute walk
    """Calculate how many destinations reachable within distance"""
    reach = {}
    for node in G.nodes():
        # Get all nodes within distance
        reachable = nx.single_source_dijkstra_path_length(
            G, node, cutoff=distance, weight='length'
        )
        reach[node] = len(reachable)
    return reach

# Calculate 800m reach (roughly 10-minute walk)
nodes['reach_800m'] = nodes.index.map(calculate_reach(G, distance=800))




# Visualise
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 1, figsize=(12, 12))

edges.plot(ax=ax, color='lightgrey', linewidth=0.5)
nodes.plot(column='reach_800m', 
           ax=ax, 
           cmap='viridis', 
           markersize=20,
           legend=True,
           legend_kwds={'label': 'Number of reachable nodes (800m)'})

ax.set_title('Walkable Reach in Auckland CBD', fontsize=14)
ax.set_axis_off()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()


Figure 3



High-reach locations are well-connected – you can walk to many destinations from there. These locations often show higher pedestrian activity because they’re convenient starting points or destinations.


Building footprint analysis (optional)
If you have building footprint data, momepy can calculate building-level metrics:

# Load buildings
buildings = gpd.read_file("data/auckland_buildings.gpkg")

# Calculate building area
buildings['area'] = buildings.geometry.area

# Calculate perimeter
buildings['perimeter'] = buildings.geometry.length

# Calculate form factor (compactness)
# More compact = closer to circular
buildings['form_factor'] = (4 * np.pi * buildings['area']) / (buildings['perimeter'] ** 2)

# Calculate orientation
buildings['orientation'] = momepy.Orientation(buildings).series

# Buildings elongated north-south vs east-west can affect microclimates
# and walking comfort

title: 2.4 Urban analytics indicators
text:
Connecting to your assignment
Let’s bring this together for analysing pedestrian footfall:
Hypothesis generation: Based on the indicators we’ve computed, we can form testable hypotheses:

Density hypothesis: Areas with higher population density should show higher pedestrian footfall (more nearby residents).
Centrality hypothesis: Streets with higher betweenness centrality should show higher footfall (more through-traffic).
Access hypothesis: Areas near parks or other amenities might show different temporal patterns (weekend spikes?).


Example analysis workflow

# Load your pedestrian count data
footfall = pd.read_csv("data/pedestrian_counts_2023.csv")

# Join with street network centrality data
footfall_with_centrality = footfall.merge(
    nodes[['betweenness', 'reach_800m']], 
    left_on='sensor_location',
    right_index=True,
    how='left'
)




# Analyse relationship
import seaborn as sns

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 5))

# Plot 1: Centrality vs footfall
sns.scatterplot(data=footfall_with_centrality, 
                x='betweenness', 
                y='daily_count',
                alpha=0.6,
                ax=axes[0])
axes[0].set_xlabel('Betweenness Centrality')
axes[0].set_ylabel('Daily Pedestrian Count')
axes[0].set_title('Network Centrality vs Footfall')

# Plot 2: Reach vs footfall
sns.scatterplot(data=footfall_with_centrality, 
                x='reach_800m', 
                y='daily_count',
                alpha=0.6,
                ax=axes[1])
axes[1].set_xlabel('Walkable Reach (800m)')
axes[1].set_ylabel('Daily Pedestrian Count')
axes[1].set_title('Walkable Accessibility vs Footfall')

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

# Calculate correlation
print(f"Correlation with betweenness: {footfall_with_centrality[['betweenness', 'daily_count']].corr().iloc[0,1]:.3f}")
print(f"Correlation with reach: {footfall_with_centrality[['reach_800m', 'daily_count']].corr().iloc[0,1]:.3f}")


Figure 4









For your blog post



You might write something like:

“Queen Street shows consistently higher footfall than other CBD locations, which makes sense given its network position. Our analysis reveals a betweenness centrality score of 0.28, compared to an average of 0.12 for other CBD streets – meaning it sits on 2.3 times more shortest paths through the network. This isn’t just about people shopping on Queen Street; it’s about everyone who needs to get through the CBD.”

title: 2.4 Urban analytics indicators
text:
Key takeaways and responsible interpretation

Always state your units. Is that persons/km² or persons/hectare? Metres or kilometres?
Acknowledge limitations. Straight-line distance isn’t walking distance. Betweenness centrality assumes people take shortest paths (they don’t always).
Context matters. A “walkable” distance in Auckland might differ from Singapore or Helsinki based on climate, culture, and urban form.
Correlation ≠ causation. High centrality streets might have high footfall, but this doesn’t mean improving centrality will automatically increase pedestrian activity.
Temporal dynamics. Urban indicators are often static (density, network structure), but phenomena like pedestrian movement are highly dynamic. Your assignment asks you to explore these temporal patterns – which is where things get really interesting!

These morphological characteristics are relatively stable, making them excellent controls for understanding what changed about human behaviour rather than the city itself.

Your First Python Code
Let’s start with the traditional first programme:
print("Hello World")
This simple command displays text on the screen. The print() function is one of Python’s most useful built-in functions.

Adding Comments
Comments help document your code. Python supports two types:
# This is a single-line comment

'''

Write Clear Comments

Python as a Calculator

# Addition
1 + 1  # Returns: 2

title: 2.1. Basic Python
text:
Python Syntax Essentials

End-of-Line Terminates Statements
In Python, the end of a line marks the end of a statement:
temperature = 5
This is an assignment operation, where we create a variable named temperature and assign it the value 5.
If you need a statement to continue to the next line, use the backslash (\):
x = 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + \
    5 + 6 + 7 + 8


Whitespace Within Lines
Whitespace within lines doesn’t matter for Python’s interpretation:
x=1+2
x = 1 + 2
x             =        1    +                2
All three lines are equivalent, but which is most readable? The second option with consistent spacing is preferred.


Indentation Matters!
Unlike many languages, Python uses indentation to define code blocks:
# Correct indentation
if temperature > 25:
    print("It's hot!")
    print("Stay hydrated!")

# Incorrect - will cause an error
if temperature > 25:
print("It's hot!")  # IndentationError!






Consistent Indentation



Always use 4 spaces for indentation (most editors can convert Tab to spaces automatically). Mixing tabs and spaces will cause errors.




Parentheses (Round Brackets)
Parentheses have multiple uses in Python:

Grouping mathematical operations:

2 * (3 + 4)  # Returns: 14

Calling functions:

print('first value:', 1)
len('Hello World')

Executing methods:

L = [4, 2, 3, 1]
L.sort()  # Parentheses execute the sort method
print(L)  # Output: [1, 2, 3, 4]

title: 2.1. Basic Python
text:
Variables and Assignment
A variable stores values for later use. Think of it as a labelled box in computer memory.
weather = "Freezing"
print(weather)  # Output: Freezing

temperature = 15
print(temperature)  # Output: 15

Variables as Pointers
Variables in Python are references (pointers) to objects in memory:
x = [1, 2, 3]
y = x  # Both x and y point to the same list

# Modifying the list through x
x.append(4)
print(y)  # Output: [1, 2, 3, 4] - y sees the change!

# Reassigning x
x = 'something else'
print(y)  # Output: [1, 2, 3, 4] - y is unchanged
This behaviour is important when working with data structures in geospatial analysis.

title: 2.1. Basic Python
text:
Data Types

Everything Is an Object
Python is an object-oriented language. Every entity has:

Attributes: Data associated with the object
Methods: Functions that operate on the object

x = 4
type(x)  # Returns: <class 'int'>

x = 'hello'
type(x)  # Returns: <class 'str'>

x = 3.14159
type(x)  # Returns: <class 'float'>


Basic Data Types
Python has four fundamental data types:



Type
Description
Example




int
Whole numbers
4, -17, 0


float
Decimal numbers
3.1415, -2.5


str
Text strings
'Hello', "Auckland"


bool
True/False values
True, False





Working with Strings
Strings represent text data:
city = "Auckland"
print(city)  # Output: Auckland

# Length of string
len(city)  # Returns: 8

# String concatenation
greeting = "Hello, " + city
print(greeting)  # Output: Hello, Auckland

# String repetition
print(city * 3)  # Output: AucklandAucklandAuckland

# Case transformations
print(city.upper())  # Output: AUCKLAND
print(city.lower())  # Output: auckland






String Methods



Strings have many useful methods. Access them with dot notation:
text = "  Hello World  "
text.strip()     # Remove whitespace: "Hello World"
text.replace("World", "Python")  # Replace text
text.split()     # Split into list: ["Hello", "World"]




Working with Numbers
my_int = 2
my_float = 24.3

# Mixing int and float gives float
my_int + my_float  # Returns: 26.3 (float)

# Division always returns float
10 / 5  # Returns: 2.0 (not 2)

# Floor division returns int
10 // 3  # Returns: 3

# Modulus returns remainder
10 % 3  # Returns: 1

# Exponentiation
2**3  # Returns: 8


Boolean Values
Booleans represent truth values and are essential for conditional logic:
x = 5
y = 4

# Comparison returns boolean
print(x > y)      # Output: True
print(not(x > y)) # Output: False
print(x == y)     # Output: False
print(x != y)     # Output: True

Boolean Operations
Combine boolean values with logical operators:



Operator

title: 2.1. Basic Python
text:
For Loops
Loops allow you to repeat operations efficiently. They’re essential for processing multiple data items.

Basic For Loop Syntax
for variable in collection:
    do_something_with_variable
Key points: - The loop statement must end with a colon (:) - Code inside the loop must be indented (4 spaces) - No special end statement needed—just return to normal indentation


Example: Iterating Through a List
western_line = ["Britomart", "Parnell", "Newmarket", "Grafton",
                "Mt Eden", "Kingsland", "Morningside", "Baldwin Ave"]

for station in western_line:
    print(station)
Output:
Britomart
Parnell
Newmarket
Grafton
Mt Eden
Kingsland
Morningside
Baldwin Ave


Using Range
The range() function generates sequences of numbers:
# Print numbers 0 to 4
for value in range(5):
    print(value)

# Output:
# 0
# 1
# 2
# 3
# 4


Working with Multiple Lists
cities = ["Helsinki", "Stockholm", "Oslo", "Reykjavik", "Copenhagen"]
countries = ["Finland", "Sweden", "Norway", "Iceland", "Denmark"]

# Iterate using indices
for i in range(len(cities)):
    print(cities[i], "is the capital of", countries[i])

# Output:
# Helsinki is the capital of Finland
# Stockholm is the capital of Sweden
# Oslo is the capital of Norway
# Reykjavik is the capital of Iceland
# Copenhagen is the capital of Denmark






Real-World Application



In geospatial analysis, you’ll use loops to: - Process multiple data files - Calculate statistics for each region - Create maps for different time periods - Apply transformations to all features in a dataset

title: 2.1. Basic Python
text:
Conditional Statements
Conditional statements allow your code to make decisions based on conditions.

If-Else Structure
temperature = 17

if temperature > 25:
    print("It's hot!")
else:
    print("It's not hot!")
    
# Output: It's not hot!


If Without Else
Sometimes you only need action when a condition is true:
temperature = 17

if temperature > 25:
    print(temperature, "is greater than 25")

# No output because condition is False


If-Elif-Else
Use elif (else if) for multiple conditions:
temperature = -3

if temperature > 0:
    print(temperature, "degrees celsius is above freezing")
elif temperature == 0:
    print(temperature, "degrees celsius is at the freezing point")
else:
    print(temperature, "degrees celsius is below freezing")

# Output: -3 degrees celsius is below freezing
Python checks conditions in order and executes the first true block.


Comparison with Strings
weather = "rain"

if weather == "rain":
    print("Wear a raincoat!")
else:
    print("No raincoat needed.")

# Output: Wear a raincoat!

title: 2.1. Basic Python
text:
Combining Conditions
Use and and or to create complex conditions:
weather = "rain"
wind_speed = 14
comfort_limit = 10

# Multiple conditions with 'or'
if (weather == "rain") or (wind_speed >= comfort_limit):
    print("Just stay at home")
else:
    print("Go out and enjoy the weather!")

# Output: Just stay at home

title: 2.1. Basic Python
text:
Combining Loops and Conditionals
One of the most powerful patterns in programming:
temperatures = [0, 12, 17, 28, 30]

# Check each temperature
for temperature in temperatures:
    if temperature > 25:
        print(temperature, "is hot")
    else:
        print(temperature, "is not hot")

# Output:
# 0 is not hot
# 12 is not hot
# 17 is not hot
# 28 is hot
# 30 is hot

Practical Example: Processing Sensor Data
sensor_readings = [15.2, 23.1, 45.7, 12.8, 38.9]
threshold = 30.0

high_readings = []

for reading in sensor_readings:
    if reading > threshold:
        high_readings.append(reading)
        print(f"Alert: Reading {reading} exceeds threshold!")

print(f"\nTotal high readings: {len(high_readings)}")

title: 2.1. Basic Python
text:
Methods and Dot Notation
Objects in Python have methods—functions that belong to the object:
L = [1, 2, 3]

# Append method adds an item
L.append(100)
print(L)  # Output: [1, 2, 3, 100]

# Check if a float is an integer
x = 4.5
x.is_integer()  # Returns: False

x = 4.0
x.is_integer()  # Returns: True
The dot (.) connects the object to its method: object.method()

title: 2.1. Basic Python
text:
Practical Exercise: Auckland Transport
Let’s combine everything we’ve learned:
# Auckland transport data
stations = ["Britomart", "Newmarket", "Mt Eden", "Henderson"]
daily_passengers = [15000, 8500, 6200, 4100]
target = 7000

print("Auckland Transport Station Analysis")
print("=" * 40)

# Analyse each station
for i in range(len(stations)):
    station = stations[i]
    passengers = daily_passengers[i]
    
    print(f"\n{station} Station:")
    print(f"  Daily passengers: {passengers:,}")
    
    # Check if station meets target
    if passengers >= target:
        print(f"  ✓ Meets target ({target:,} passengers)")
        
        # Further categorisation
        if passengers >= 10000:
            print("  Status: High volume station")
        else:
            print("  Status: Medium volume station")
    else:
        shortfall = target - passengers
        print(f"  ✗ Below target by {shortfall:,} passengers")
        print("  Status: Low volume station")

# Summary statistics
total_passengers = sum(daily_passengers)
average_passengers = total_passengers / len(daily_passengers)

print("\n" + "=" * 40)
print(f"Total daily passengers: {total_passengers:,}")
print(f"Average per station: {average_passengers:,.0f}")

title: 2.1. Basic Python
text:
Next Steps
Now that you understand Python basics, you’re ready to work with tabular data in ?sec-dataframes, where you’ll learn to use pandas for data manipulation—an essential skill for geospatial analysis.

title: 2.2. DataFrames
text:
What is a DataFrame?
A DataFrame is a two-dimensional tabular data structure with labelled rows and columns—essentially a spreadsheet in Python. It’s the most common way to work with structured data.






Figure 1: DataFrame structure showing rows (observations) and columns (variables)



DataFrames can be thought of as: - A table with rows and columns - A collection of Series (columns) that share an index - A dictionary where each key is a column name

title: 2.2. DataFrames
text:
Dictionaries: Building Blocks
Before diving into DataFrames, let’s understand dictionaries—Python’s key-value data structure that underpins much of pandas.

Dictionary Basics
A dictionary stores data as key:value pairs:
# Create a dictionary
city_populations = {
    "Auckland": 1672000,
    "Wellington": 217200,
    "Christchurch": 389700
}

# Access values by key
print(city_populations["Auckland"])  # Output: 1672000

# Add a new entry
city_populations["Hamilton"] = 185000

# Modify an existing value
city_populations["Auckland"] = 1700000


Dictionary Methods
# Get all keys
city_populations.keys()
# Output: dict_keys(['Auckland', 'Wellington', 'Christchurch', 'Hamilton'])

# Get all values
city_populations.values()
# Output: dict_values([1700000, 217200, 389700, 185000])

# Get key-value pairs
city_populations.items()
# Output: dict_items([('Auckland', 1700000), ('Wellington', 217200), ...])


Iterating Through Dictionaries
# Iterate through keys
for city in city_populations.keys():
    print(city)

# Iterate through key-value pairs
for city, population in city_populations.items():
    print(f"{city}: {population:,}")

# Output:
# Auckland: 1,700,000
# Wellington: 217,200
# Christchurch: 389,700
# Hamilton: 185,000


Nested Dictionaries
Dictionaries can contain other dictionaries or lists—useful for complex data:
staff = {
    "people": [
        {"name": "Hyesop", "role": "lecturer"},
        {"name": "Sila", "role": "lecturer"},
        {"name": "Oliver", "role": "tutor"}
    ],
    "pets": [
        {"name": "Pepper", "species": "dog"},
        {"name": "Pip", "species": "dog"},
        {"name": "Harriet", "species": "cat"}
    ]
}

# Access nested data
print(staff["people"][0]["name"])  # Output: Hyesop






Why Dictionaries Matter for GIS



Geospatial data formats like GeoJSON are built on nested dictionaries:
{
  "type": "Feature",
  "geometry": {"type": "Point", "coordinates": [174.76, -36.85]},
  "properties": {"name": "Auckland", "population": 1672000}
}

title: 2.2. DataFrames and Pandas
text:
Getting Started with Pandas

What is pandas?
pandas is Python’s data analysis library. It provides: - DataFrame: A table with rows and columns (like Excel) - Series: A single column of data - Operations for filtering, grouping, merging data
Think of it as “Excel in Python, but more powerful and reproducible.”


Installation and Import
# Install with uv (if not already installed)
# uv add pandas

# Import with standard alias
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np  # Often used together






Standard Aliases



The Python community uses these aliases consistently: - pandas → pd - numpy → np - matplotlib.pyplot → plt - seaborn → sns - geopandas → gpd (you’ll see this in Section 2.4!)
Using standard aliases makes your code readable to other Python users.

title: 2.2. DataFrames and Pandas
text:
Creating DataFrames

What is a DataFrame?
A DataFrame is a two-dimensional table with: - Rows (observations/records) - Columns (variables/fields) - Index (row labels, usually numbers)



DataFrame structure


GIS context: Think of it as an attribute table without the geometry column (yet—that comes in Section 2.4 with GeoPandas).


From a Dictionary (The Key Connection!)
This is where dictionaries and DataFrames connect:
# Step 1: Create a dictionary (Section 2.2 beginning!)
city_data = {
    'city': ['Auckland', 'Wellington', 'Christchurch', 'Hamilton', 'Tauranga'],
    'population': [1672000, 217200, 389700, 185000, 158000],
    'area_km2': [1086, 444, 608, 877, 135],
    'region': ['Auckland', 'Wellington', 'Canterbury', 'Waikato', 'Bay of Plenty']
}

# Step 2: Convert to DataFrame
cities_df = pd.DataFrame(city_data)

# Step 3: View it
print(cities_df)
Output:
          city  population  area_km2           region
0     Auckland     1672000      1086         Auckland
1   Wellington      217200       444       Wellington
2  Christchurch      389700       608        Canterbury
3     Hamilton      185000       877          Waikato
4     Tauranga      158000       135  Bay of Plenty
Notice: - Each dictionary key becomes a column name - Each list in the dictionary becomes a column - Pandas automatically adds an index (0, 1, 2, 3, 4)


From a List of Dictionaries
Sometimes data comes as multiple dictionaries (common from APIs):
# Auckland parks (like an API might return)
parks_list = [
    {"name": "Albert Park", "area_ha": 6.0, "suburb": "Auckland CBD"},
    {"name": "Victoria Park", "area_ha": 7.5, "suburb": "Auckland CBD"},
    {"name": "Myers Park", "area_ha": 4.0, "suburb": "Auckland CBD"},
    {"name": "Western Springs", "area_ha": 43.0, "suburb": "Westmere"}
]

# Convert to DataFrame
parks_df = pd.DataFrame(parks_list)
print(parks_df)
Output:
              name  area_ha        suburb
0      Albert Park      6.0  Auckland CBD
1    Victoria Park      7.5  Auckland CBD
2       Myers Park      4.0  Auckland CBD
3  Western Springs     43.0      Westmere
This is exactly what you’ll do with GeoJSON! Each feature becomes a row.

title: 2.2. DataFrames and Pandas
text:
Reading Data Files

CSV Files
CSV (Comma-Separated Values) is the most common format for tabular data.
Basic reading:
# Read local file
df = pd.read_csv('auckland_buses.csv')

# Read from URL
url = 'https://example.com/data.csv'
df = pd.read_csv(url)
Common arguments:
# Specify separator (default is comma)
df = pd.read_csv('data.txt', sep='\t')  # Tab-separated
df = pd.read_csv('data.csv', sep=';')   # Semicolon-separated

# Skip rows at the beginning (e.g., metadata lines)
df = pd.read_csv('data.csv', skiprows=2)  # Skip first 2 rows

# Specify which row is the header
df = pd.read_csv('data.csv', header=0)    # First row (default)
df = pd.read_csv('data.csv', header=None) # No header row

# Specify data types for columns
df = pd.read_csv('data.csv', dtype={'population': int, 'name': str})

# Handle missing values
df = pd.read_csv('data.csv', na_values=['NA', 'missing', '-', ''])

# Use a specific column as index
df = pd.read_csv('data.csv', index_col='city_name')

# Parse dates automatically
df = pd.read_csv('data.csv', parse_dates=['date_column'])

# Read only certain columns
df = pd.read_csv('data.csv', usecols=['city', 'population', 'area'])

# Read only first n rows
df = pd.read_csv('data.csv', nrows=100)

# Specify encoding (for non-UTF-8 files)
df = pd.read_csv('data.csv', encoding='utf-8')
df = pd.read_csv('data.csv', encoding='latin-1')  # Sometimes needed for old files
Practical example:
# Reading Auckland bus route data with specific settings
buses = pd.read_csv(
    'auckland_buses.csv',
    sep=',',                    # Comma-separated
    skiprows=1,                 # Skip metadata line
    header=0,                   # Next row is header
    dtype={
        'route_number': str,    # Keep as string (e.g., "70")
        'daily_riders': int,
        'route_length': float
    },
    na_values=['NA', 'missing'],
    parse_dates=['start_date'],
    usecols=['route_number', 'route_name', 'daily_riders', 'route_length']
)

print(buses.head())
print(buses.dtypes)  # Check data types


Excel Files
# Read Excel file
df = pd.read_excel('data.xlsx')

# Specify sheet by name
df = pd.read_excel('data.xlsx', sheet_name='Sheet1')

# Specify sheet by index (0-based)
df = pd.read_excel('data.xlsx', sheet_name=0)

# Read all sheets into a dictionary
all_sheets = pd.read_excel('data.xlsx', sheet_name=None)
print(all_sheets.keys())  # See all sheet names

# Other arguments work similarly to read_csv
df = pd.read_excel(
    'auckland_demographics.xlsx',
    sheet_name='Suburbs',
    skiprows=2,
    usecols='A:D',  # Columns A through D
    dtype={'population': int}
)


JSON Files
Perfect for working with API responses and GeoJSON!
# Read JSON file
df = pd.read_json('data.json')

# Read from URL (API endpoint)
api_url = 'https://api.example.com/auckland/parks'
df = pd.read_json(api_url)

# For nested JSON (like GeoJSON), you might need to normalize
import json

# Read GeoJSON
with open('auckland_parks.geojson', 'r') as f:
    geojson = json.load(f)

# Extract properties into DataFrame
features = geojson['features']
properties_list = [f['properties'] for f in features]
df = pd.DataFrame(properties_list)

print(df)


Saving DataFrames
# Save to CSV
df.to_csv('output.csv', index=False)  # index=False avoids extra column

# Save to Excel
df.to_excel('output.xlsx', sheet_name='Data', index=False)

# Save to JSON
df.to_json('output.json', orient='records', indent=2)

# Save with specific encoding
df.to_csv('output.csv', encoding='utf-8', index=False)

title: 2.2. DataFrames and Pandas
text:
Exploring DataFrames

Initial Inspection
# Create sample Auckland suburb data
suburbs = pd.DataFrame({
    'suburb': ['Mt Eden', 'Parnell', 'Grey Lynn', 'Ponsonby', 'Epsom', 'Newmarket'],
    'population': [15200, 8400, 11300, 9800, 18900, 8200],
    'median_income': [78000, 92000, 65000, 88000, 105000, 95000],
    'avg_house_price': [1.2, 1.8, 1.1, 1.6, 2.1, 1.9],  # millions NZD
    'parks_count': [3, 2, 4, 3, 5, 2]
})

# View first rows
print(suburbs.head())      # First 5 rows (default)
print(suburbs.head(3))     # First 3 rows

# View last rows
print(suburbs.tail())      # Last 5 rows
print(suburbs.tail(2))     # Last 2 rows

# Random sample
print(suburbs.sample(3))   # 3 random rows


DataFrame Properties
# Shape: (rows, columns)
print(suburbs.shape)  # (6, 5)

# Dimensions
print(f"Rows: {len(suburbs)}")
print(f"Columns: {len(suburbs.columns)}")

# Column names
print(suburbs.columns)
# Output: Index(['suburb', 'population', 'median_income', 'avg_house_price', 'parks_count'])

# Data types
print(suburbs.dtypes)
Output:
suburb                object
population             int64
median_income          int64
avg_house_price      float64
parks_count            int64
dtype: object


Summary Statistics
# Summary statistics for numeric columns
print(suburbs.describe())
Output:
       population  median_income  avg_house_price  parks_count
count        6.00           6.00             6.00         6.00
mean     11966.67       87166.67             1.62         3.17
std       4419.69       14658.87             0.41         1.17
min       8200.00       65000.00             1.10         2.00
25%       8850.00       80500.00             1.25         2.25
50%      11050.00       90000.00             1.55         3.00
75%      15500.00       93750.00             1.88         3.75
max      18900.00      105000.00             2.10         5.00
Interpretation: - count: Number of non-null values - mean: Average - std: Standard deviation (spread) - min, 25%, 50%, 75%, max: Quartiles
Custom statistics:
# Specific statistic for a column
print(suburbs['population'].mean())      # 11966.67
print(suburbs['population'].median())    # 11050.0
print(suburbs['population'].std())       # 4419.69
print(suburbs['population'].sum())       # 71800

# Multiple statistics at once
print(suburbs['avg_house_price'].agg(['mean', 'median', 'min', 'max']))


Information Summary
# Comprehensive info about DataFrame
print(suburbs.info())
Output:
<class 'pandas.core.frame.DataFrame'>
RangeIndex: 6 entries, 0 to 5
Data columns (total 5 columns):
 #   Column             Non-Null Count  Dtype  
---  ------             --------------  -----  
 0   suburb             6 non-null      object 
 1   population         6 non-null      int64  
 2   median_income      6 non-null      int64  
 3   avg_house_price    6 non-null      float64
 4   parks_count        6 non-null      int64  
dtypes: float64(1), int64(3), object(1)
memory usage: 368.0+ bytes
This tells you: - Total rows and columns - Which columns have missing values - Data types - Memory usage

title: 2.2. DataFrames and Pandas
text:
Selecting Data

Selecting Columns
# Single column (returns Series)
pop_series = suburbs['population']
print(type(pop_series))  # <class 'pandas.core.series.Series'>

# Single column (returns DataFrame)
pop_df = suburbs[['population']]
print(type(pop_df))  # <class 'pandas.core.frame.DataFrame'>

# Multiple columns
subset = suburbs[['suburb', 'population', 'median_income']]
print(subset)


Selecting Rows by Index
Using .iloc[] (integer location):
# Single row by position
first_row = suburbs.iloc[0]  # First row
print(first_row)

# Multiple rows by position
first_three = suburbs.iloc[0:3]  # Rows 0, 1, 2
print(first_three)

# Specific rows
selected = suburbs.iloc[[0, 2, 4]]  # Rows 0, 2, 4
print(selected)

# Rows and columns together
subset = suburbs.iloc[0:3, 0:2]  # First 3 rows, first 2 columns
print(subset)
Using .loc[] (label-based):
# Single row by index label
row = suburbs.loc[0]

# Multiple rows
rows = suburbs.loc[0:2]  # Includes row 2 (unlike iloc!)

# Specific columns
subset = suburbs.loc[:, ['suburb', 'population']]

# Rows and columns
subset = suburbs.loc[0:2, ['suburb', 'population']]
Difference between .iloc and .loc: - .iloc[0:3] → rows 0, 1, 2 (excludes 3) - .loc[0:3] → rows 0, 1, 2, 3 (includes 3 if it exists)


Boolean Indexing (Filtering)
This is the most powerful selection method! It uses conditionals from Section 2.1.
# Find wealthy suburbs (income > 90000)
wealthy = suburbs[suburbs['median_income'] > 90000]
print(wealthy)

# Find affordable housing (price < 1.5M)
affordable = suburbs[suburbs['avg_house_price'] < 1.5]
print(affordable)

# Multiple conditions (AND) - use &
wealthy_and_affordable = suburbs[
    (suburbs['median_income'] > 80000) & 
    (suburbs['avg_house_price'] < 1.5)
]
print(wealthy_and_affordable)

# Multiple conditions (OR) - use |
edge_suburbs = suburbs[
    (suburbs['population'] < 9000) | 
    (suburbs['population'] > 18000)
]
print(edge_suburbs)

# Using .isin() for multiple values
cbd_suburbs = suburbs[suburbs['suburb'].isin(['Mt Eden', 'Parnell', 'Newmarket'])]
print(cbd_suburbs)

# String methods
parks_many = suburbs[suburbs['suburb'].str.contains('Park')]  # Contains "Park"
starts_with_p = suburbs[suburbs['suburb'].str.startswith('P')]  # Starts with P


The .query() Method
Cleaner syntax for filtering:
# Simple condition
wealthy = suburbs.query('median_income > 90000')

# Multiple conditions
ideal = suburbs.query('median_income > 80000 and avg_house_price < 1.8')

# Using variables (with @)
threshold = 90000
high_income = suburbs.query('median_income > @threshold')

# String matching
parnell = suburbs.query('suburb == "Parnell"')

title: 2.2. DataFrames
text:
Adding and Modifying Columns

Creating New Columns
# From calculation
df['Age_in_months'] = df['Age'] * 12

# From existing columns
df['Full_info'] = df['Name'] + ' from ' + df['City']

# Conditional values
df['Category'] = 'Adult'  # Set all to 'Adult'
df.loc[df['Age'] < 18, 'Category'] = 'Minor'  # Override for minors

# Using apply with a function
def age_group(age):
    if age < 18:
        return 'Youth'
    elif age < 65:
        return 'Adult'
    else:
        return 'Senior'

df['Age_Group'] = df['Age'].apply(age_group)


Practical Example: Processing Pedestrian Data
# Calculate hourly average from minute counts
pedestrians['hourly_average'] = pedestrians['total_count'] / 60

# Create time period categories
def classify_time(hour):
    if 6 <= hour < 9:
        return 'Morning Rush'
    elif 9 <= hour < 12:
        return 'Morning'
    elif 12 <= hour < 14:
        return 'Lunch'
    elif 14 <= hour < 17:
        return 'Afternoon'
    elif 17 <= hour < 20:
        return 'Evening Rush'
    else:
        return 'Night'

pedestrians['time_period'] = pedestrians['hour'].apply(classify_time)

# Flag weekends
pedestrians['is_weekend'] = pedestrians['day_of_week'] >= 5

# Calculate change from previous measurement
pedestrians['count_change'] = pedestrians['count'].diff()

title: 2.2. DataFrames and Pandas
text:
Grouping and Aggregation
Grouping is one of pandas’ most powerful features. It follows the split-apply-combine pattern.

Basic Grouping
# Add region column to our data
suburbs['region'] = ['Central', 'Eastern', 'Western', 'Western', 'Central', 'Central']

# Calculate average population by region
avg_pop_by_region = suburbs.groupby('region')['population'].mean()
print(avg_pop_by_region)
Output:
region
Central    14100.0
Eastern     8400.0
Western    10550.0
Name: population, dtype: float64


Multiple Aggregations
# Multiple statistics for one column
region_stats = suburbs.groupby('region')['population'].agg(['mean', 'sum', 'count'])
print(region_stats)
Output:
              mean     sum  count
region                          
Central   14100.0  42300      3
Eastern    8400.0   8400      1
Western   10550.0  21100      2


Aggregating Multiple Columns
# Different aggregations for different columns
summary = suburbs.groupby('region').agg({
    'population': ['mean', 'sum'],
    'median_income': 'mean',
    'avg_price_millions': ['mean', 'max'],
    'num_parks': 'sum'
})

print(summary)


Custom Aggregation Functions
# Define custom function
def price_range(prices):
    return prices.max() - prices.min()

# Use it in groupby
price_ranges = suburbs.groupby('region')['avg_price_millions'].agg([
    'mean',
    ('range', price_range),
    'count'
])
print(price_ranges)


Practical Example: Auckland Transport Routes
# Auckland bus and train routes
routes = pd.DataFrame({
    'route_name': ['Inner Link', 'Outer Link', 'Eastern Line', 'Western Line', 
                   'City Link', 'Northern Express'],
    'mode': ['Bus', 'Bus', 'Train', 'Train', 'Bus', 'Bus'],
    'daily_riders': [12000, 8500, 22000, 18500, 15000, 9800],
    'route_length_km': [6.5, 8.2, 28.0, 22.0, 4.2, 15.0]
})

# Calculate riders per km
routes['efficiency'] = routes['daily_riders'] / routes['route_length_km']

# Group by transport mode
mode_summary = routes.groupby('mode').agg({
    'daily_riders': ['sum', 'mean'],
    'route_length_km': 'mean',
    'efficiency': 'mean'
}).round(2)

print("\nTransport Mode Summary:")
print(mode_summary)

title: 2.2. DataFrames
text:
Reshaping Data: Melt and Pivot

Melt: Wide to Long Format
Convert wide data (multiple value columns) to long format:
# Wide format
df_wide = pd.DataFrame({
    'City': ['Auckland', 'Wellington', 'Christchurch'],
    'Jan_Temp': [25, 22, 20],
    'Feb_Temp': [24, 21, 19],
    'Mar_Temp': [23, 20, 18]
})

# Convert to long format
df_long = pd.melt(
    df_wide,
    id_vars=['City'],           # Columns to keep
    var_name='Month',            # Name for variable column
    value_name='Temperature'     # Name for value column
)

print(df_long)
Output:
          City      Month  Temperature
0     Auckland   Jan_Temp           25
1   Wellington   Jan_Temp           22
2  Christchurch   Jan_Temp           20
3     Auckland   Feb_Temp           24
4   Wellington   Feb_Temp           21
...


Pivot: Long to Wide Format
# Convert back to wide format
df_pivot = df_long.pivot(
    index='City',
    columns='Month',
    values='Temperature'
)






When to Melt



Melting is useful when: - You have multiple columns representing the same type of data - You want to use groupby or plot with seaborn - Your data needs to be in “tidy” format for analysis

title: 2.2. DataFrames and Pandas
text:
Handling Missing Data
Real-world data is messy. Here’s how to handle it.

Detecting Missing Data
# Create data with missing values
suburbs_missing = pd.DataFrame({
    'suburb': ['Mt Eden', 'Parnell', 'Grey Lynn', 'Ponsonby'],
    'population': [15200, None, 11300, 9800],
    'median_income': [78000, 92000, None, 88000],
    'avg_price': [1.2, 1.8, 1.1, None]
})

# Check for missing values
print(suburbs_missing.isnull())
print(suburbs_missing.isnull().sum())  # Count per column
print(suburbs_missing.isnull().sum().sum())  # Total missing
Output:
   suburb  population  median_income  avg_price
0   False       False          False      False
1   False        True          False      False
2   False       False           True      False
3   False       False          False       True

suburb           0
population       1
median_income    1
avg_price        1
dtype: int64

Total: 3


Removing Missing Data
# Drop rows with ANY missing values
clean = suburbs_missing.dropna()
print(clean)

# Drop rows where specific column is missing
clean = suburbs_missing.dropna(subset=['population'])

# Drop columns with ANY missing values
clean = suburbs_missing.dropna(axis=1)


Filling Missing Data
# Fill with a specific value
filled = suburbs_missing.fillna(0)

# Fill with column mean
suburbs_missing['population'] = suburbs_missing['population'].fillna(
    suburbs_missing['population'].mean()
)

# Fill with column median
suburbs_missing['median_income'] = suburbs_missing['median_income'].fillna(
    suburbs_missing['median_income'].median()
)

# Forward fill (use previous value)
filled = suburbs_missing.fillna(method='ffill')

# Backward fill (use next value)
filled = suburbs_missing.fillna(method='bfill')

# Fill different columns with different values
suburbs_missing = suburbs_missing.fillna({
    'population': suburbs_missing['population'].median(),
    'median_income': suburbs_missing['median_income'].mean(),
    'avg_price': suburbs_missing['avg_price'].median()
})


Interpolation
For time series or ordered data:
# Linear interpolation
suburbs_missing['population'] = suburbs_missing['population'].interpolate(method='linear')


Best Practices






Handling Missing Data Thoughtfully



Before removing or filling: 1. Understand WHY data is missing - Random (safe to fill) - Systematic (e.g., sensor failure - investigate) - By design (e.g., not applicable)

Document your approach
Consider creating a “missing” indicator column
Report how many values you handled

For GIS: Missing coordinates or key identifiers usually mean dropping that record. Missing attributes might be fillable.

title: 2.2. DataFrames
text:
Merging and Joining DataFrames
Combining data from multiple sources is common in geospatial analysis.

Types of Joins






Figure 3: Different types of joins




Inner: Only matching rows from both DataFrames
Left: All rows from left DataFrame, matching from right
Right: All rows from right DataFrame, matching from left
Outer: All rows from both DataFrames



Merge Example
# Create two DataFrames
df1 = pd.DataFrame({
    'ID': [1, 2, 3, 4],
    'Name': ['Tom', 'Nick', 'Krish', 'Jack'],
    'Age': [20, 21, 19, 18]
})

df2 = pd.DataFrame({
    'ID': [3, 4, 5, 6],
    'Subject': ['Maths', 'English', 'Science', 'History'],
    'Score': [88, 75, 90, 85]
})

# Inner join (only matching IDs: 3, 4)
inner = pd.merge(df1, df2, on='ID', how='inner')

# Left join (all from df1)
left = pd.merge(df1, df2, on='ID', how='left')

# Outer join (all from both)
outer = pd.merge(df1, df2, on='ID', how='outer')


Practical Example: Combining Pedestrian and Location Data
# Pedestrian counts
counts = pd.DataFrame({
    'location_id': [1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3],
    'hour': [8, 9, 8, 9, 8, 9],
    'count': [150, 200, 300, 350, 100, 120]
})

# Location details
locations = pd.DataFrame({
    'location_id': [1, 2, 3, 4],
    'location_name': ['Queen St', 'Karangahape Rd', 'Ponsonby Rd', 'Broadway'],
    'district': ['CBD', 'CBD', 'Ponsonby', 'Newmarket']
})

# Merge to add location names
merged = pd.merge(counts, locations, on='location_id', how='left')
print(merged)

Practical Example: Visualising Pedestrian Patterns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns

# Set style
sns.set_style('whitegrid')

# 1. Time series of counts
plt.figure(figsize=(12, 4))
hourly_avg = pedestrians.groupby('hour')['count'].mean()
hourly_avg.plot()

# 3. Heatmap of location x hour

    values='count',
    index='location',
    columns='hour',

# 4. Compare time periods

period_stats = pedestrians.groupby('time_period')['count'].mean().sort_values()
period_stats.plot(kind='barh', color='steelblue')

title: 2.2. DataFrames
text:
Practical Workflow Example
Here’s a complete workflow analysing Auckland pedestrian data:
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns

# 1. Read and explore data
pedestrians = pd.read_csv('auckland_pedestrian_counts.csv')
print("Dataset shape:", pedestrians.shape)
print("\nFirst few rows:")
print(pedestrians.head())

# 2. Data cleaning
# Check for missing values
print("\nMissing values:")
print(pedestrians.isnull().sum())

# Fill missing counts with median
pedestrians['count'].fillna(pedestrians['count'].median(), inplace=True)

# Remove any remaining rows with critical missing data
pedestrians.dropna(subset=['location', 'datetime'], inplace=True)

# 3. Feature engineering
# Convert datetime
pedestrians['datetime'] = pd.to_datetime(pedestrians['datetime'])
pedestrians['hour'] = pedestrians['datetime'].dt.hour
pedestrians['day_of_week'] = pedestrians['datetime'].dt.dayofweek
pedestrians['is_weekend'] = pedestrians['day_of_week'] >= 5

# Create time period categories
def classify_time(hour):
    if 6 <= hour < 9:
        return 'Morning Rush'
    elif 9 <= hour < 12:
        return 'Morning'
    elif 12 <= hour < 14:
        return 'Lunch'
    elif 14 <= hour < 17:
        return 'Afternoon'
    elif 17 <= hour < 20:
        return 'Evening Rush'
    else:
        return 'Night'

pedestrians['time_period'] = pedestrians['hour'].apply(classify_time)

# 4. Analysis
# Find busiest locations
busiest_locations = pedestrians.groupby('location')['count'].agg([
    'mean', 'median', 'max', 'count'
]).sort_values('mean', ascending=False)
print("\nBusiest locations:")
print(busiest_locations.head())

# Compare weekday vs weekend
day_type_stats = pedestrians.groupby('is_weekend')['count'].agg([
    'mean', 'median', 'std'
]).round(0)
print("\nWeekday vs Weekend:")
print(day_type_stats)

# Peak hours by location
peak_hours = pedestrians.groupby('location').apply(
    lambda x: x.loc[x['count'].idxmax(), ['hour', 'count']]
)
print("\nPeak hours by location:")
print(peak_hours)

# 5. Visualisation
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(14, 10))

# Hourly pattern
hourly_avg = pedestrians.groupby('hour')['count'].mean()
axes[0, 0].plot(hourly_avg.index, hourly_avg.values, marker='o')
axes[0, 0].set_title('Average Count by Hour')
axes[0, 0].set_xlabel('Hour of Day')
axes[0, 0].set_ylabel('Average Count')
axes[0, 0].grid(True, alpha=0.3)

# Top locations
top_10 = busiest_locations.head(10)['mean']
axes[0, 1].barh(range(len(top_10)), top_10.values)
axes[0, 1].set_yticks(range(len(top_10)))
axes[0, 1].set_yticklabels(top_10.index)
axes[0, 1].set_title('Top 10 Busiest Locations')
axes[0, 1].set_xlabel('Average Count')

# Weekday vs weekend distribution
pedestrians.boxplot(column='count', by='is_weekend', ax=axes[1, 0])
axes[1, 0].set_title('Weekday vs Weekend Distribution')
axes[1, 0].set_xlabel('Is Weekend')
axes[1, 0].set_ylabel('Count')

# Time period comparison
period_avg = pedestrians.groupby('time_period')['count'].mean().sort_values()
axes[1, 1].barh(range(len(period_avg)), period_avg.values, color='steelblue')
axes[1, 1].set_yticks(range(len(period_avg)))
axes[1, 1].set_yticklabels(period_avg.index)
axes[1, 1].set_title('Average Count by Time Period')
axes[1, 1].set_xlabel('Average Count')

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

# 6. Export results
# Save cleaned data
pedestrians.to_csv('pedestrians_cleaned.csv', index=False)

# Save summary statistics
busiest_locations.to_csv('location_summary.csv')

print("\nAnalysis complete!")

title: 4  Geospatial Data
text:
4.2 What is GIS?
Roger Tomlinson coined the term “GIS” (Geographic Information Systems), defining it as:

A computer system for capturing, storing, checking, and displaying data related to positions on Earth’s surface.

All data in GIS are georeferenced, meaning each feature has:

Attribute information: What it is (name, type, value, etc.)
Spatial information: Where it is (coordinates, location)


4.2.1 GIS Applications
GIS enables us to answer complex spatial questions. For example, with crime data we can explore:

Where are the most vulnerable communities located?
Why do crimes occur in one area and not another?
How do offenders travel to crime locations?
Where are there more or fewer stop and searches than expected?

title: 4  Geospatial Data
text:
4.3 Types of Maps

4.3.1 Reference Maps
Reference maps are used to communicate location and static data points:

Purpose: To ‘pin point’ data on a map
Nature: Descriptive
Examples: Road maps, topographic maps, navigation tools



4.3.2 Thematic Maps
Thematic maps highlight spatial relationships and patterns:

Purpose: To ‘study a theme’ within spatial data
Nature: Explanatory
Examples: Choropleth maps, heat maps, cartograms







Rail Maps: Reference or Thematic?



Transport maps like Auckland’s rail network can be both:

Reference: They show station locations and line routes
Thematic: They can reveal patterns in life expectancy, poverty, or house prices along transport corridors

title: 4  Geospatial Data
text:
4.4 Geospatial Data Types

4.4.1 Vector Data
Vector data represents discrete features using points, lines, and polygons:

Points: Individual locations (cities, sensors, trees)
Lines: Linear features (roads, rivers, routes)
Polygons: Areas with boundaries (parcels, countries, lakes)

Vector data is preferred in social sciences because human settlements and processes tend to have discrete borders.


4.4.2 Raster Data
Raster data represents continuous surfaces using a grid of pixels:

Each pixel has a value
Commonly used for: satellite imagery, elevation models, temperature surfaces
Dominated in environmental sciences due to remote sensing

title: 4  Geospatial Data
text:
4.5 File Formats

4.5.1 Vector Formats

Shapefile (.shp): Traditional GIS format (requires multiple files: .shp, .shx, .dbf, .prj)
GeoJSON (.geojson): Web-friendly, human-readable format
GeoPackage (.gpkg): Modern, single-file format supporting multiple layers
KML/KMZ: Google Earth format



4.5.2 Raster Formats

GeoTIFF (.tif): Standard format with embedded spatial information
NetCDF: Multi-dimensional arrays (climate data)
HDF5: Hierarchical data format

title: 4  Geospatial Data
text:
4.6 Coordinate Reference Systems (CRS)

4.6.1 Understanding Projections
The Earth is a 3D sphere (technically an oblate spheroid), but maps are 2D. This creates distortion.
Common CRS systems:

EPSG:4326 (WGS84): Unprojected geographic coordinates (latitude/longitude in degrees)
EPSG:3857: Web Mercator (used by Google Maps, metres)
EPSG:2193: NZTM (New Zealand Transverse Mercator, metres)







CRS Matters!



Always check and match CRS when combining datasets. Mixing CRS will give incorrect results.

title: 4  Geospatial Data
text:
4.7 Working with GeoPandas

4.7.1 Installation and Setup
import geopandas as gpd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from shapely.geometry import Point, LineString, Polygon


4.7.2 Reading Spatial Data
# Read from various formats
countries = gpd.read_file('countries.shp')
cities = gpd.read_file('cities.geojson')
regions = gpd.read_file('regions.gpkg')

# Read from URL
url = 'https://example.com/data.geojson'
gdf = gpd.read_file(url)


4.7.3 Exploring GeoDataFrames
# View first few rows
countries.head()

# Check the CRS
countries.crs

# Get column information
countries.columns

# Summary statistics
countries.describe()

# Access geometry column
countries.geometry


4.7.4 Basic Operations

4.7.4.1 Filtering Data
# Filter by attribute
oceania = countries[countries['continent'] == 'Oceania']

# Filter by spatial relationship
# Select countries that contain a specific point
auckland = Point(174.76, -36.85)
nz = countries[countries.contains(auckland)]


4.7.4.2 Creating Geometries
# Create a point
point = Point(174.76, -36.85)

# Create a line
line = LineString([(174.76, -36.85), (174.77, -36.86)])

# Create a polygon
polygon = Polygon([(0, 0), (1, 0), (1, 1), (0, 1)])

# Create a GeoDataFrame from scratch
gdf = gpd.GeoDataFrame(
    {'name': ['Auckland'], 
     'population': [1672000]},
    geometry=[Point(174.76, -36.85)],
    crs='EPSG:4326'
)

title: 4  Geospatial Data
text:
4.8 Spatial Relationships
GeoPandas provides functions to test spatial relationships:

contains(): Does geometry A contain geometry B?
within(): Is geometry A within geometry B?
intersects(): Do geometries A and B intersect?
touches(): Do geometries share a boundary but not area?
crosses(): Do geometries cross each other?
overlaps(): Do geometries overlap partially?
disjoint(): Are geometries completely separate?


4.8.1 Example: Finding Which Country Contains a City
# Create a point for New York
new_york = Point(-74.006, 40.7128)

# Find the country containing New York
country_with_ny = countries[countries.contains(new_york)]
print(country_with_ny['name'].values)  # Output: ['United States']

# Test if New York is within the USA
usa = countries[countries['name'] == 'United States'].geometry.iloc[0]
new_york.within(usa)  # Returns: True

title: 4  Geospatial Data
text:
4.9 Spatial Joins
Spatial joins combine attributes from two datasets based on spatial relationships:
# Join cities to countries based on spatial location
joined = gpd.sjoin(
    cities,           # Left GeoDataFrame
    countries,        # Right GeoDataFrame
    predicate='within',  # Spatial relationship
    how='left'        # Join type (left, right, inner)
)

# Now cities have country attributes
print(joined[['city_name', 'country_name', 'continent']])

4.9.1 Common Spatial Join Use Cases

Assigning census data to geographic units
Finding which administrative area a point falls within
Counting features within polygons
Aggregating data by spatial location

title: 4  Geospatial Data
text:
4.10 Coordinate Transformations

4.10.1 Reprojecting Data
# Check current CRS
print(gdf.crs)

# Reproject to a different CRS
gdf_projected = gdf.to_crs('EPSG:3857')  # Web Mercator

# Reproject to match another dataset
gdf_matched = gdf.to_crs(other_gdf.crs)






When to Reproject




For distance/area calculations: Use a projected CRS (in metres)
For web mapping: Use EPSG:3857
For spatial operations: Ensure all datasets have the same CRS

title: 4  Geospatial Data
text:
4.11 Geometric Operations

4.11.1 Buffering
Create a zone around features:
# Create 10km buffer around cities (data must be in metres)
cities_projected = cities.to_crs('EPSG:3857')
cities_buffered = cities_projected.copy()
cities_buffered['geometry'] = cities_buffered.buffer(10000)  # 10km in metres


4.11.2 Dissolve
Combine features based on an attribute:
# Dissolve countries by continent
continents = countries.dissolve(by='continent', aggfunc='sum')


4.11.3 Overlay Operations
Combine geometries from two datasets:
# Intersection: areas where both datasets overlap
intersection = gpd.overlay(gdf1, gdf2, how='intersection')

# Union: all areas from both datasets
union = gpd.overlay(gdf1, gdf2, how='union')

# Difference: areas in gdf1 not in gdf2
difference = gpd.overlay(gdf1, gdf2, how='difference')

title: 4  Geospatial Data
text:
4.12 Visualisation

4.12.1 Basic Plotting
# Simple plot
countries.plot()

# Customised plot
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 10))
countries.plot(ax=ax, 
               column='pop_est',      # Colour by population
               cmap='YlOrRd',         # Colour scheme
               legend=True,           # Show legend
               edgecolor='black')     # Border colour
ax.set_title('World Population by Country')
plt.show()


4.12.2 Choropleth Maps
# Create a classified choropleth map
countries.plot(column='gdp_per_capita',
               scheme='quantiles',     # Classification scheme
               k=5,                    # Number of classes
               cmap='viridis',
               legend=True,
               legend_kwds={'title': 'GDP per Capita (Quantiles)'})


4.12.3 Multiple Layers
# Plot multiple layers together
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 8))

# Base layer
countries.plot(ax=ax, color='lightgrey', edgecolor='black')

# Add cities
cities.plot(ax=ax, color='red', markersize=20, alpha=0.6)

ax.set_title('World Countries and Major Cities')
ax.set_axis_off()
plt.show()

title: 4  Geospatial Data
text:
4.13 The Modifiable Areal Unit Problem (MAUP)
MAUP refers to the sensitivity of statistical results to the choice of spatial units:

Scale Effect: Changing the size of spatial units affects results
Zoning Effect: Different arrangements of the same-sized units produce different results







Be Aware of MAUP



When aggregating or analysing spatial data, remember that your choice of geographic units can influence your findings. Always consider whether your results might change with different spatial aggregations.

title: 4  Geospatial Data
text:
4.14 Practical Exercise

4.14.1 Example: Analysing New Zealand Regions
# Load NZ regional data
nz_regions = gpd.read_file('nz_regions.gpkg')

# Check CRS
print(nz_regions.crs)

# Reproject to NZTM for accurate measurements
nz_regions = nz_regions.to_crs('EPSG:2193')

# Calculate area in square kilometres
nz_regions['area_km2'] = nz_regions.geometry.area / 1_000_000

# Calculate population density
nz_regions['pop_density'] = (nz_regions['population'] / 
                               nz_regions['area_km2'])

# Find regions within 100km of Auckland
auckland_point = gpd.GeoDataFrame(
    {'name': ['Auckland']},
    geometry=[Point(1756673, 5917750)],  # NZTM coordinates
    crs='EPSG:2193'
)

# Buffer Auckland
auckland_buffer = auckland_point.buffer(100000)  # 100km

# Spatial join
nearby_regions = nz_regions[
    nz_regions.intersects(auckland_buffer.iloc[0])
]

# Visualise
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 12))
nz_regions.plot(ax=ax, column='pop_density', 
                cmap='YlOrRd', legend=True)
auckland_buffer.plot(ax=ax, facecolor='none', 
                     edgecolor='blue', linewidth=2)
plt.title('NZ Population Density and 100km Buffer from Auckland')
plt.show()
